summary: You produced a working brute-force solution for standard cases and correctly avoided reusing the same element by starting j at i+1. However, you missed an edge-case expectation from the test harness (empty input / no-solution should return []), leading to a thrown exception and a failed edge test. You also identified the optimal hash-map approach but didn’t implement it, leaving the solution at O(n^2) despite constraints up to 1e5.

test_results.summary_note: All basic tests passed; one edge case failed due to raising ValueError on empty/no-solution input instead of returning [].

dimensions.what_to_improve: Match the required/observed contract for empty/no-solution inputs (return [] instead of raising), and add an explicit early return for len(nums) < 2 to prevent edge failures.

primary_focus: Implement the single-pass hash map (complement lookup) solution and default to returning [] for empty/no-solution inputs to meet both performance expectations and test-harness contracts.
thinking_and_logic: You approached the problem with a correct brute-force baseline, iterating over all unique index pairs (i < j) and returning as soon as a matching sum is found. This is logically sound and prevents using the same element twice. The main gaps were (1) not aligning the function’s behavior with the test expectation for empty/no-solution inputs (you raised instead of returning []), and (2) not upgrading to the canonical O(n) approach despite recognizing it, which matters under the given large-n constraints.
code_assessment: Your final code matches the answer key’s brute_force approach (nested loops, O(n^2) time, O(1) space). Compared to the canonical optimal solution, you missed the core technique: a hash map of previously seen values to indices, checking target - nums[i] in O(1) average time per element. The optimal approach achieves O(n) time and is the expected solution for nums.length up to 1e5, while the brute-force approach risks timeouts and is less competitive in interviews. Separately, the test failure shows a contract mismatch: raising a ValueError on empty/no-solution input is not accepted by the harness, which expects [].

next_steps.action: Rewrite Two Sum using a single-pass hash map (value -> index) and check complement before inserting.
next_steps.why: This is the canonical optimal solution (O(n) time, O(n) space) and aligns with typical interview expectations for large inputs.
next_steps.how: Initialize seen = {}; for i, x in enumerate(nums): c = target - x; if c in seen: return [seen[c], i]; else: seen[x] = i; return [] at the end.

next_steps.action: Adopt a standard edge-case checklist and decide/announce a fallback contract before coding.
next_steps.why: You were prompted about unusual inputs, but still shipped a version that failed the empty input case; a checklist prevents avoidable misses.
next_steps.how: Before submitting, quickly verify: len(nums) < 2, empty list, no-solution behavior (return []), duplicates (e.g., [3,3], target=6), negatives, and large values.

next_steps.action: Practice the sorted-array variant using two pointers.
next_steps.why: It’s a common follow-up and reinforces choosing data-structure/ordering-driven strategies.
next_steps.how: With a sorted array, use l/r pointers moving inward based on sum vs target; track original indices if needed by sorting pairs (value, index).

transcript.text: Here's the problem: given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target.
Let me restate: I need two distinct indices whose values sum to the target. I'll start with the straightforward approach — check every pair with two loops — and optimize if there's time.
Writing the nested loops now. Outer loop i, inner loop from i plus one so I don't reuse the same element.
Okay, it works on the example. Running the visible tests.
Before you finish — consider whether there are any unusual inputs worth checking.
Unusual inputs... duplicates should be fine since I use indices. I think I'm good, submitting.
One of the visible tests failed — the empty input case. You raised an error instead of returning an empty list.
Ah, I see. I assumed there's always a solution because of the constraints, so I raised. I'd need a guard for empty or no-solution inputs.
What's the complexity of your solution?
Two nested loops, so O(n squared) time and constant space. I know a hash map would make it O(n) but I didn't get to it.
